options: The probability that the parameter value p is correct
The probability of the observed data if the parameter were p, viewed as a function of p
The prior belief about p
The proportion of observations equal to p
questions.why: Likelihood is P(data | parameter), read as a score for how well each parameter value explains what was seen. Getting a probability **for** the parameter requires Bayes' theorem and a prior. Confusing the two is the most common MLE mistake.

questions.q: Why do we usually maximise the **log**-likelihood rather than the likelihood itself?
options: The log-likelihood has its peak at a different, better parameter value
Software cannot compute likelihoods
The log-likelihood is always positive
Logs turn products into sums, avoid numbers too tiny for a computer and make the calculus easier, while the peak stays at the same place
questions.why: The log is always increasing, so it does not move the maximum. It turns the product of many small probabilities into a manageable sum. Log-likelihoods are usually negative (the log of a number below 1), which is fine.

questions.q: Help-desk calls in five one-hour slots are 3, 5, 4, 6, 2. Under a Poisson model, what is the maximum likelihood estimate of λ?
options: 4 calls per hour
20 calls per hour
5 calls per hour
2.5 calls per hour
questions.why: For a Poisson model the slope of the log-likelihood, (sum of counts) / λ − n, is zero at λ̂ = 20 / 5 = 4: the sample mean. 20 is the total, not the rate; 5 is the number of slots.

questions.q: Five measurements are 4, 6, 8, 10, 12. What is the maximum likelihood estimate of the variance under a normal model?
questions.why: The MLE divides the sum of squared deviations (40) by n: 40 / 5 = 8. The unbiased sample variance divides by n − 1 and gives 10. 2.83 and 3.16 are standard deviations, not variances.

questions.q: For 7 conversions out of 10, the log-likelihood at p = 0.7 is −6.11, a small negative number. A colleague says "the model fits badly because the likelihood is so tiny". What is wrong with this?
options: Nothing; a likelihood of 0.0022 means a poor fit
The likelihood is the probability of one exact sequence, which is always tiny; only relative values across parameter values (or models on the same data) are meaningful
Log-likelihoods should always be positive
The MLE must be wrong, since p = 0.5 would give a larger likelihood
questions.why: L(0.7) = 0.0022 is small because any particular sequence of 10 outcomes is unlikely. MLE compares values: 0.7 beats 0.5 (0.00098) and 0.9 (0.00048). Log-likelihoods of probabilities below 1 are naturally negative.

questions.q: A new product page has 1 conversion from its first visitor. The MLE of the conversion rate is 100%. What is the best way to handle this?
options: Trust it; MLE is unbiased
Divide by n − 1 instead
Recognise that MLE overfits tiny samples; collect more data or add prior information (a Bayesian estimate) that pulls the rate towards a sensible base rate
Round it down to 50%
questions.why: MLE uses only the evidence, so with one observation it jumps to the extreme. With lots of data, MLE and Bayesian estimates agree; with little data, a prior keeps estimates sensible. The n − 1 correction applies to variances, not proportions.

questions.q: Model A has maximised log-likelihood −120 with 3 parameters; model B has −118 with 6 parameters. Which does AIC prefer?
options: Model B, because its log-likelihood is higher
They are tied
Model A: AIC = 246 versus 248 for B
Model B: AIC = 236 versus 240
questions.why: AIC = 2k − 2 ln L. A: 6 + 240 = 246. B: 12 + 236 = 248. Lower is better, so A wins: B's gain of 2 log-likelihood units does not pay for 3 extra parameters. 236 versus 240 forgets the parameter penalty.

questions.q: In an interview: "How is logistic regression's log-loss related to maximum likelihood?"
options: They are unrelated; log-loss is just a convenient error measure
Log-loss is minimised by ordinary least squares
Log-loss is the likelihood of the coefficients being correct
Minimising log-loss is exactly maximising the Bernoulli (yes/no) likelihood of the observed labels, so logistic regression is MLE in disguise
questions.why: Log-loss is the negative average log-likelihood of yes/no outcomes, so its minimum is the MLE. Just as squared error corresponds to normal errors (OLS), log-loss corresponds to yes/no outcomes. There is no closed form, so an optimiser does the climbing.
